slices.label: Men outside the South
slices.source: 1890 and 1900 censuses interpolated to November 1896; men 21+ outside the eleven Southern states (including declarant aliens where they could vote); turnout and choice from the backbone, calibrated to certified 1896 returns.

slices.label: Women outside the South
slices.source: 1890 and 1900 censuses interpolated to November 1896; women 21+ outside the South; women could vote for president only in Wyoming, Colorado (1893) and Utah (statehood, January 1896); Idaho's amendment was adopted at this same election, so Idaho women first voted in 1898.

slices.label: White Southerners
slices.source: 1890 and 1900 censuses interpolated to November 1896; white adults in the eleven former Confederate states (includes a small number of American Indian and Asian adults); calibrated to certified 1896 returns.

slices.label: Black Southerners
slices.source: 1890 and 1900 censuses interpolated to November 1896; Black adults in the eleven former Confederate states; disfranchisement was intensifying (Mississippi 1890, South Carolina 1895, poll taxes and registration laws elsewhere); the shortfall against white turnout is counted as exclusion.

slices.label: Immigrants not yet citizens
slices.source: 1890 and 1900 censuses interpolated to November 1896; foreign-born white adults who were aliens or had only declared their intent (first papers); declarant aliens could vote in several Midwestern and Western states (fewer each decade as states repealed it), so part of this slice could vote.

runs.summary: Rerun with nothing changed, 1896 comes out as it did: McKinley wins, 271–176. The closest state was Kentucky, which went to McKinley by 0.1 points. Every one of my 100 reruns reproduces it exactly.
howIGotThis: The numbers: the 1890 and 1900 census counts interpolated to 1896 and certified returns; every draw reproduces 1896 exactly before the change.
How sure: I reran it 100 times with different population and parameter draws.

south-white.name: Anna Reed
south-white.quote: I wish I could have a say in who leads this country, but the law doesn't allow women to vote. That's just how things are.
south-white.controlQuote: I wish I could have a say in who leads this country, but the law doesn't allow women to vote. That's just how things are.

women.name: Ruth Robinson
women.quote: I wish I could have a say in it, but that's not how things are. My husband will cast our ballot tomorrow.

men.name: Ernest Reed
men.quote: The Republicans say they'll bring back protection and good wages. After what we've seen with all the strikes and hard times, that sounds better than more silver talk.
